# DISTRIBUTED DELIVERY
## Communication, collaboration and conflict standards for cross-continental project teams
**Companion operating standard to *Where and How We Work* v2.0 | v2.0 (complete draft) | Work Design Council adoption sought; Executive Committee ratification sought on §4.4 only**

**Decision sought:**
1. **Work Design Council:** adoption of the standards (§§5–13), the four named roles (§14), and the five-rung conflict ladder (§11).
2. **Executive Committee:** ratification that the mandatory **Communication Addendum** (Appendix A) is an *implementation specification under existing Spine commitment S2*, not a ninth Spine commitment — and that its scope is limited to teams meeting the distributed test in §4.4.
3. **Both:** funding of the Gate 1 measurement wave (§15).

All quantities in this document are calibration targets and return to the Council for approval before anything is communicated to employees.

---

## §0.0 Glossary (for readers without v2.0 in hand)

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Subsidiarity Rule** | Parent framework's governing constraint: each decision is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects, and no lower. |
| **Layer 1 / Global Spine (S1–S8)** | Eight non-waivable global commitments set by the Executive Committee. Capped at eight. Relevant here: **S2** every team has a written published Charter; **S3** written-first for decisions, specs and context (explicitly *not* for 1:1s, coaching, feedback, wellbeing); **S4** meetings opt-in for information, opt-out for decisions; **S5** one time-zone tax, shared; **S6** same job, same access; **S7** baseline environment guarantee; **S8** nothing that breaks local law, tax status or a collective agreement. |
| **Layer 2 / Country Dial** | Country- or region-level settings: legal floor, core hours, language of record, stipends, works-council agreements. |
| **Layer 3 / Team Charter** | The real unit of decision. Written by each team of ~6–15 people, published, reviewed semi-annually. |
| **Work Modes M1–M5** | M1 deep focus; M2 convergent (someone must change their mind); M3 divergent (nobody knows the answer yet); M4 apprenticeship/tacit transfer; M5 coordination and handoff. |
| **Overlay T / Overlay C** | T = trust formation, funded as capacity not hoped for as a byproduct. C = customer/site/shift override on location. |
| **Populations A / B / C** | A = location-flexible; B = fixed-location (plant, warehouse, retail, lab, clinical, field); C = mixed. |
| **DRI** | Directly Responsible Individual — the single named person accountable for a decision or artefact. |
| **Gate 1** | The parent framework's measurement gate: replaces design targets with measured values before any policy is published. |
| **Exception Register** | Central log of approved departures from the framework, each with owner, remedy and review date. |
| **Work Design Council** | Cross-functional adjudication body created by parent §15; breaks ties between the five ranked objectives. |

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**These teams do not have a communication problem. They have an architecture problem that presents as a communication problem, and the standard response — more channels, more standups, more tooling — reliably makes it worse.** "Delays and misunderstandings" is symptom vocabulary; underneath it sit **seven distinct failure modes** — latency, ambiguity, decision re-litigation, unshared time-zone tax, cultural misread, relational deficit, and language asymmetry (§1) — each with a different and sometimes opposite remedy. So the first deliverable is not a practice; it is a **triage instrument** that tells a team which failure mode it actually has, with a confirming measurement for each (§3). The remedies are then: **(a)** a published **response-latency contract** measured in the *responder's* working hours, plus engineered **handoff packets** borrowed wholesale from shift-handover practice in our own plants (§5); **(b)** **deliberate time-zone architecture** — one of four topologies chosen on the arithmetic, not inherited from hiring history, and the arithmetic is unforgiving: our own named hubs of Bengaluru, Stuttgart and Salt Lake City share **no hour of common working time at all** (§6.2), which means "add a daily all-hands standup" is not a hard option but an impossible one; **(c)** a **federated source of truth** — canonical index plus jurisdictionally sited stores — because a single global repository is illegal or unreachable in several of our markets and S8 is a hard gate (§7.1); **(d)** **language architecture treated as an equity mechanism**, not an etiquette note (§8.1); **(e)** a **Team Culture Map** built from individual self-description and never from a country-to-dimension lookup table (§8.2); **(f)** **trust as funded capacity** with a named rule against unsupported solo-in-region placement (§10); and **(g)** a **five-rung conflict ladder with timeboxes and a structural screen at every rung**, on the working hypothesis that a large share of what arrives as personality clash is a decision-rights defect wearing a face (§11). Two disciplines run through all of it: every measurement is a **team-level diagnostic and is prohibited as an individual performance input** (§5.5), and every load-bearing empirical claim is **labelled as a hypothesis with a Gate 1 test** (§1.3), because the parent framework holds itself to that standard and a companion document that does not will not be believed.

---

## §0 Scope, status, and fit with the parent framework

### 0.1 Status of the numbers, and of the claims

Two disciplines, both inherited:

- **Numbers.** Every latency target, hour-count, ratio, budget and timebox is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, marked *[target]* on first use per section. Gate 1 replaces them.
- **Claims.** Every load-bearing causal or empirical assertion is numbered **H1, H2…** and listed in §15.2 with the measurement that would falsify it. The parent document flagged its own central claim (that M1 and M5 dominate knowledge-work weeks) as "a hypothesis, not a finding." This document does not get to be more confident than its parent about things it has not measured.

### 0.2 What this document is

*Where and How We Work* v2.0 decides **who decides** where work happens. It does not tell a team split across Bengaluru, Stuttgart and Salt Lake City how to ship a thing together. This document does. It is the **Layer-3 implementation manual** for distributed project teams, plus the **Layer-2 constraints** that countries and regions must set for it to function.

It is deliberately not a culture programme, a tool selection, or a training curriculum. Those follow from it; none of them substitutes for it.

### 0.3 Mapping to the parent framework

| Parent element | What this document adds | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **S2 — every team has a published Charter** | The Communication Addendum, which *replaces and expands* three existing Charter fields rather than sitting beside them | §4.2, App. A |
| **S3 — written-first** | Federated artefact taxonomy, decision-record standard, silence semantics, commitment language, documentation-debt ledger | §7 |
| **S3's exclusions (1:1s, coaching, feedback, wellbeing not documented)** | Carried forward unchanged, and **the tension with grievance record-keeping is resolved, not deferred**: metadata is recorded, content is not | §11.7 |
| **S4 — meeting discipline** | Mode-to-channel mapping including asynchronous video, pre-read discipline, distributed-facilitation standard, required inventory fields | §9 |
| **S5 — one time-zone tax, shared** | Overlap arithmetic, four topologies, rotation mechanics, unsociable-hours ledger that makes the Standing Exception auditable, on-call legality | §5.4, §6 |
| **S6 — same job, same access** | Participation-asymmetry and hub-bias metrics; distance-to-promotion parity reporting with minimum cell sizes | §12 |
| **S7 — baseline environment guarantee** | Connectivity and audio floor as a *communication* prerequisite, not a comfort item | §6.6 |
| **S8 — local law is a hard gate** | Federated source-of-truth pattern; on-call as working time; monitoring consultation | §7.1, §5.4, §5.5 |
| **§4 modes and overlays** | Mode-to-channel mapping; Overlay T converted from aspiration into funded capacity with allocation logic | §9.1, §10 |
| **§15 Council / Exception Register** | Rung-4 structural referral: escalations that turn out to be decision-rights defects route to the Council, not to Employee Relations | §11.6 |
| **Appendix C decision rights** | Delta table | §16 |

### 0.4 Scope of population — and the direction of learning

Populations A, B and C all appear. Distributed *project* teams are predominantly A and C.

The previous draft framed population B as an exclusion ("a warehouse team cannot hold an asynchronous pre-read"). That was both a straw man and a missed insight, and it is withdrawn. **The direction of practice transfer runs B → A, not A → B with apologies.** Shift handover in our plants, nursing handover in our clinical operations, and turnover logs in field maintenance are century-old, well-instrumented disciplines for exactly the problem knowledge workers have just discovered: transferring live work across a boundary without losing state. §5.3's handoff packet is a deliberate lift from SBAR-style clinical handover and plant turnover sheets, and we should say so.

Where a practice genuinely cannot travel to B, §13 states the equivalent grant or states plainly that none exists. Wherever this document reports a fairness metric, all three populations appear in the cut (§12.3).

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

"Communication delays and occasional misunderstandings" is a **composite symptom**. Treated as one thing it attracts one intervention — usually a tool, sometimes a mandate to overlap — and both fail, because at least seven mechanisms are in play and several of them have opposite remedies. Adding synchronous contact helps a team with a relational deficit and actively harms a team with an ambiguity problem, because it moves specification back into unrecorded speech.

### 1.1 The seven failure modes

| # | Failure mode | What it looks like | What it actually is | Wrong fix | Right fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **F1** | **Latency** | "Asked Tuesday, answered Friday, shipped a week late" | No published response contract; questions batched into the wrong channel | Force overlap; add standups | Response-latency classes + handoff packets (§5) |
| **F2** | **Ambiguity** | Two sites built to two readings of the same sentence | Specification and commitment language are uncalibrated | "Communicate more" | Commitment Language Standard + Severity Lexicon + spec templates (§7.4) |
| **F3** | **Decision re-litigation** | The same decision made three times in three regions | Decisions unwritten, or written where the other region cannot find them | More meetings | Decision records + federated source of truth + DRI naming (§7.2–7.3) |
| **F4** | **Unshared time-zone tax** | One region always on the 22:00 call; that region goes quiet, then attrites | A distributional injustice, not an attitude problem | Resilience training | Topology choice + rotation + unsociable-hours ledger (§6) |
| **F5** | **Cultural misread** | Silence read as consent; directness read as contempt; escalation read as betrayal | Divergent, unwritten norms about feedback, hierarchy, disagreement and silence | Awareness e-learning | Team Culture Map → written team norms (§8.2) |
| **F6** | **Relational deficit** | Text read in the least charitable available tone | Insufficient relational credit to absorb ordinary friction | Virtual happy hours | Funded Overlay T cadence + onboarding redesign (§10) |
| **F7** | **Language asymmetry** | The same three fluent speakers decide everything; others "had no comments" | Fast idiomatic synchronous speech is a competence tax on non-native speakers, and it silently reallocates influence | Ask people to speak up | Language architecture: written-first as equaliser, no-idiom norms, captions and transcripts by default, speaking-order rotation, interpretation budget (§8.1) |

F7 was absent from v1.0 and is the most consequential addition. It is separate from F5 because the remedies are different and cheaper: F5 requires negotiated norms, F7 requires channel and facilitation design. Conflating them produces culture training where a caption track and a written agenda would have done more.

### 1.2 Three corollaries

**Corollary 1 — Volume is not the variable.** Our working expectation **[H1]** is that teams reporting the worst communication show *higher*, not lower, message and meeting volume. Adding channels to a team suffering F2 or F3 is actively harmful: ambiguity replicates and re-litigation accelerates. This is a testable claim, not a slogan, and §3 gives the measurement.

*(The v1.0 formulation "more communication is the disease's most common presentation" is withdrawn as logically confused. The precise claim is narrower and survives scrutiny: **excess undifferentiated volume is a symptom that is routinely mistaken for the cure.** This document itself prescribes a substantial quantity of new communication norms; the defence is that norms reduce volume by removing the need to negotiate expectations transaction by transaction.)*

**Corollary 2 — Distance does not create misunderstanding; it removes the cheap repair.** Co-located teams misunderstand each other constantly and repair it in four seconds at a desk. Distributed teams discover the same misunderstanding a week later, downstream, expensive. Our expectation **[H2]** is that the underlying misunderstanding *rate* is similar and the *detection latency* is what differs by an order of magnitude.

> **Therefore the design goal is not fewer misunderstandings. It is shorter time-to-detection.**

Read every practice in §5 and §7 as detection-latency reduction, not defect-rate reduction. This single reframe changes what you build: you stop trying to write perfect specifications and start building cheap, fast contradiction detectors — confidence labels, do-not-touch fields, decision records that a distant reader trips over, handoff packets that fail loudly.

**Corollary 3 — Most reported interpersonal conflict in cross-border teams is structural.** An engineer who believes a counterpart is obstructive is usually looking at a person with contradictory instructions from a second reporting line, no decision right over the thing being asked of them, and a 21:00 call. Mediating that relationship is a category error: it asks two people to be nicer about a defect neither of them owns.

*Correcting v1.0:* no target is set on this share. Setting a target on a *diagnostic classification* creates pressure to reclassify in order to hit it, which is precisely the failure we are trying to prevent. Instead: the structural-screen outcome (§11.4) is **measured and reported**, with a **monitored range** *[expected range 25–55% of Rung-2 escalations — Gate 1 to establish the baseline]*. A rate outside the range in either direction triggers a review of screening quality, not a push on the number.

### 1.3 Register of hypotheses

H1 (volume/quality inverse), H2 (detection latency dominates defect rate), and the further hypotheses raised in §5.6 (vertical slicing beats horizontal layering), §6.3 (chained topology outperforms forced-simultaneity on cycle time), §8.1 (participation asymmetry tracks language status more strongly than seniority) and §11.5 (structural share of escalations) are consolidated in **§15.2** with a named measurement each. None of them is presented to the Council as established.

# WHERE AND HOW WE WORK
## A global operating framework for flexible work
**Executive Committee decision document | v2.0**
**Decision sought: adoption of the *structure* and the decision rights. All quantities are calibrated at Gate 1 and returned to this Committee for approval.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop trying to write one work policy for the whole company.** A single global rule — "three days in office," "remote-first," "hybrid" — will be simultaneously too loose for the teams that need co-presence to function and too tight for the teams that don't, and it will be illegal, unaffordable or culturally illegible in a meaningful share of our countries. Instead, adopt a **federated model with three layers**: a thin, non-waivable **Global Spine** (eight commitments that make us one company); a **Country Dial** set by each market against a published dossier of legal, infrastructural and normative constraints; and a **Team Charter** — the real unit of decision — written by every team of roughly 6–15 people and reviewed twice a year. Work is designed against **five work modes and two overlays** (§4), not against days of the week. Offices are re-typed from desk inventory into a **four-format portfolio** whose feasibility depends on one piece of machinery we have never had: **cross-team anchor-day allocation** (§9.2). Roughly [X]% of our workforce cannot choose where they work at all; they are in scope from page one, not as an afterthought (§6). Fairness — proximity bias, geographic pay, apprenticeship — is engineered explicitly (§11), and output measurement is fixed *before* flexibility scales, because otherwise presence quietly becomes the proxy again (§12). **One constraint governs everything: the Subsidiarity Rule (§3) — each decision is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects, and no lower.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every ratio, day-count, square-metre figure, stipend value and threshold in this document is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use in each section. They are included because a framework with no numbers cannot be argued with, and an unarguable framework cannot be improved. **Gate 1 (§16) replaces them with measured values**; the Committee approves the calibrated set before any policy is communicated to employees.

What we are asking the Committee to adopt today is: the three-layer structure, the eight Spine commitments, the five modes, the four office formats, the decision-rights matrix (Appendix C), the gate sequence, and the funding of Gate 1.

### 0.2 Who this covers

The phrase "future of work" has been used inside the company as a synonym for "hybrid office work." That framing excludes a large minority — possibly a majority — of our people, and it is the fastest route to a two-class company.

| Population | Illustrative share *[target — Gate 1 to measure]* | What flexibility means here | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Location-flexible** | ~[40]% | Where and when, within team and country limits | §§3–5, 7–12 |
| **B. Fixed-location** — manufacturing, warehouse, retail, lab, clinical, site security, catering, field maintenance | ~[45]% | **When**, not where: schedule predictability, shift choice, roster self-scheduling, compressed weeks, time-in-lieu, leave access | §6 (parallel framework, equal status) |
| **C. Mixed** — field service, sales, engineers with lab or site dependencies, plant supervisors | ~[15]% | Site-anchored days plus flexible remainder; the *anchor* is set by the site, the remainder by the Charter | §6.3 |

**Rule of the document:** wherever this framework grants something to population A, §6 states the equivalent grant to B and C, or explains why no equivalent exists. Wherever we report a fairness metric (§11.4), all three populations appear in the cut. A benefit that only knowledge workers can consume is not a benefit; it is a differential.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The debate has been framed as *remote vs. office*. That axis is unhelpful, because it treats location as the variable when location is a **consequence**.

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How many days in the office? | What work do we do that is *degraded* by distance, and how much of it is there? |
| Is remote work productive? | Which roles have output that is legible without co-presence — and which have we simply never learned to measure? (§12) |
| How do we get people back? | What must the office be *good at* that a home desk isn't, and are our buildings currently good at it? |
| What's our policy? | Who decides, at what layer, with what evidence, and who hears the appeal? (§3, §15) |

**Corollary 1.** Attendance is not a goal. It is an input we may or may not need. A policy expressed *purely* as a day-count is a confession that the analysis wasn't done. (Day-count *bands* have exactly one legitimate use — real-estate planning and legal negotiation. That use is fenced in §7.3.)

**Corollary 2.** Most of the pain reported as "hybrid isn't working" is not about location. It is about **meeting load, unclear decision rights, documentation debt, time-zone tax and untrained managers**. Those are fixable independent of where anyone sits; they are cheaper than real estate; and they compound. **Sequence them first** (§16, Gate 2 wave 1).

---

## §2 What we are optimising for

Named explicitly, because unnamed objectives get traded away silently.

**A gate, not a priority:** *Legal, tax and collective-agreement integrity.* No arrangement that creates permanent-establishment exposure, misclassifies employment, breaches a works-council agreement or violates working-time law. This is not ranked against anything; it is a pass/fail test applied before options are compared. Legal and Tax hold a veto, not an opinion.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Equity of opportunity** | A person's promotion odds are not predicted by their distance from a headquarters, their work pattern, or their population (A/B/C) |
| **2** | **Output quality and speed** | Team-level delivery against commitments, measured per §12 |
| **3** | **Cohesion** | Enough shared context that the company can change direction without fracturing |
| **4** | **Talent access** | Hiring and retention in labour markets a full-return policy would close to us |
| **5** | **Cost discipline** | Real estate and workplace spend per employee, against the §14 bridge |

Equity outranks output because equity failures are slow, compounding and legally actionable, while output problems are visible and correctable. Cost is last because savings taken out of cohesion and equity are borrowed, not earned.

### 2.1 Adjudication — who breaks the tie

An unarbitrated priority list is decorative. Therefore:

- Conflicts between objectives are decided by the **Work Design Council** (§15.1) on a written submission that names the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A cost proposal that reduces equity or cohesion must quantify the saving *and* the harm, and propose mitigation. "It's cheaper" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **CPO + CEO** sign-off and is entered in the Exception Register (§15.3) with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions internally. Precedent is how a federated model stays coherent without a rulebook.

---

## §3 The Subsidiarity Rule and the three layers

> **Subsidiarity Rule:** Every decision about where and how work happens is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects — and no lower.

A decision affecting one team's week belongs to that team. A decision affecting statutory rights belongs to the country. A decision affecting whether two teams on different continents can ship together belongs to the centre. Pushing a decision *up* costs speed and fit; pushing it *down* costs coherence and manufactures local unfairness.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Spine** | Executive Committee | 8 commitments. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual review |
| **Country Dial** | Country lead + HR + Legal, with works council where applicable | Legal floor, stipend values, office footprint and format mix, planning band, local core hours, right-to-disconnect implementation, language of record | Semi-annual |
| **Team Charter** | Team lead with the team | Mode profile, together-time and its purpose, core overlap, response-time norms, meeting inventory, decision protocol, onboarding, inclusion check | Semi-annual, published |

Full decision rights, including who may *not* decide what, are in **Appendix C**.

### 3.1 The Global Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**S1 — Purpose before place.** Every requirement to be somewhere must name the work mode (§4) it serves. "Because it's Tuesday" is not a reason.

**S2 — Every team has a written, published Charter.** Unwritten norms are how proximity bias enters a company. If it isn't written, it isn't a norm; it's a hazard.

**S3 — Written-first for decisions, specs and context.** These live in a durable, searchable, permissioned place. *Scope limit:* S3 governs **decisions, specifications and context only**. It explicitly does **not** apply to 1:1s, coaching, sensitive feedback, performance conversations, wellbeing discussions or relationship time — documenting those would be both chilling and, in several jurisdictions, unlawful. The old formulation ("a meeting with no artefact did not happen") is withdrawn as absolutist; the replacement test is: *if a decision was made and is not written down, it will be re-made.*

**S4 — Meetings are opt-in for information, opt-out for decisions.** No standing meeting survives two quarters without explicit renewal by its owner in the Charter's meeting inventory.

**S5 — One time-zone tax, shared.** Recurring cross-region meetings rotate their inconvenience; no region is permanently the one dialling in at 22:00.
*Exception path (mandatory, because rotation is sometimes impossible):* where the counterparty is a customer, a market open, a regulator or a plant shift, a **Standing Unsociable-Hours Exception** may be granted by the regional leader for ≤12 months, renewable, entered in the Exception Register, and only with one of four compensating remedies named: (a) follow-the-sun redesign so the handoff replaces the meeting; (b) hiring or relocating for overlap; (c) time-in-lieu at a published rate; (d) an unsociable-hours allowance where local law and practice support it. An exception with no remedy is refused.

**S6 — Same job, same access.** Location and work pattern do not change eligibility for projects, promotion, sponsorship, budget or information. Where location changes *compensation*, the rule is published, zone-based and applied mechanically (§11.2).

**S7 — A baseline environment guarantee, for everyone.** Every employee has a safe, connected, ergonomically adequate place to work — at home, in a company office, at a paid third space, or **at their site**, at company cost, at levels set by the Country Dial. For population B this reads as facilities standards: rest space, lockers, connectivity, decent break areas, and equivalent per-head workplace spend. Population B must not fund population A's stipends out of its own neglected estate.

**S8 — Nothing that breaks local law, tax status or a collective agreement.** No exceptions, no goodwill workarounds, no "just for this one hire."

Eight is the ceiling. Every additional global rule must be true simultaneously in Lagos, Stuttgart, Bengaluru, São Paulo, Osaka and Salt Lake City — and very few things are.

---

## §4 The five work modes and two overlays

Modes, not days, are the design unit. Sort a team's actual month into these five, apply the overlays, and its Charter largely writes itself.

### 4.1 The five modes (mutually exclusive; every hour lands in exactly one)

| # | Mode | Discriminating test | Distance sensitivity | Best setting | Primary enabler |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M1** | **Deep focus** | One person producing; interruption is the enemy | **Negative** — co-presence usually *harms* it | **Any environment the individual controls and can reach reliably** — home study, quiet office zone, or a Touchdown site (§9.1) where home is not viable | Calendar protection; do-not-disturb norms |
| **M2** | **Convergent work** | *Someone has to change their mind or merge two positions.* Known problem, needs a decision | Low–moderate | Anywhere with good tooling; short sync after async pre-read | Pre-read + 30-min call + written decision |
| **M3** | **Divergent work** | *Nobody knows the answer yet.* Ambiguity, generation, productive conflict, whiteboarding | **High** | Same room, writable walls, 2–6 hour blocks | In-person workshop; digital canvas as an honest second-best |
| **M4** | **Apprenticeship and tacit transfer** | *Someone is learning judgement that isn't written down.* | **Very high** | Same room, sustained, with unscheduled overhearing | Co-location blocks; work-alongs; senior time budget (§11.3) |
| **M5** | **Coordination and handoff** | *Someone needs to know something at the right time.* Status, dependencies, handoffs | Low, **if disciplined** | Nowhere in particular | Written status; overlap window; single source of truth |

M2 vs M5 is the distinction teams get wrong. **Changing a mind is M2. Transferring knowledge is M5.** If a recurring meeting only transmits information, it is M5 and should be a document.

- **Overlay T — Trust formation.** Relational credit is an *investment* that makes M2 and M3 cheap, not a mode of work. It is therefore handled as a **named budget and cadence** — offsites, shared meals, travel — owned at the Charter level and funded per §14.3. Design target *[target]*: every distributed team is physically together **at least twice a year**, and no employee goes **more than six months** without being in a room with colleagues. Treating trust as a byproduct is how distributed teams die quietly.

This eliminates the double-counting that a "customer-facing mode" would have guaranteed.

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

"Communication delays and occasional misunderstandings" is a composite symptom. Treated as one thing, it attracts one intervention — usually a tool, sometimes a mandate to overlap — and both fail, because at least six mechanisms are in play and they have opposite remedies.

### 1.1 The six failure modes

| # | Failure mode | What it looks like | What it actually is | Wrong fix | Right fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **F1** | **Latency** | "I asked Tuesday, answered Friday, shipped a week late" | No published response contract; questions batched into the wrong channel | Force overlap; add standups | Response-latency classes + handoff packets (§4) |
| **F2** | **Ambiguity** | Two teams built to two readings of the same sentence | Specification and commitment language are uncalibrated | "Communicate more" | Commitment Language Standard + Severity Lexicon + spec templates (§6.4) |
| **F3** | **Decision re-litigation** | The same decision made three times in three regions | Decisions not written, or written where the other region can't find them | More meetings | Decision records + single source of truth + DRI naming (§6.2) |
| **F4** | **Unshared time-zone tax** | One region always on the 22:00 call; that region is quiet, then attrites | A distributional injustice, not an attitude problem | Resilience training | Topology choice + rotation + unsociable-hours ledger (§5) |
| **F5** | **Cultural misread** | Silence read as consent; directness read as contempt; "yes" meaning "I heard you" | Divergent, unwritten norms about feedback, hierarchy, disagreement and silence | Awareness e-learning | Team Culture Map → written norms (§7) |
| **F6** | **Relational deficit** | Text read in the least charitable available tone | Insufficient relational credit to absorb friction | Virtual happy hours | Funded Overlay T cadence + onboarding redesign (§9) |

**Corollary 1.** *Volume is not the variable.* Teams with the worst reported communication almost always have the **highest** message and meeting volume. Adding channels to a team suffering F2 or F3 makes it worse, because ambiguity replicates and re-litigation accelerates.

**Corollary 2.** *Distance does not cause misunderstanding; it removes the cheap repair.* Co-located teams misunderstand each other constantly and repair it in four seconds at a desk. Distributed teams misunderstand each other at the same rate and discover it a week later, downstream, expensive. **The design goal is not fewer misunderstandings; it is shorter time-to-detection.** Every practice in §4 and §6 should be read as a detection-latency reduction, not a defect-rate reduction.

**Corollary 3.** *Most reported interpersonal conflict in cross-border teams is structural.* An engineer who believes a counterpart is obstructive is usually looking at a person with contradictory instructions from a second reporting line, no decision right over the thing being asked for, and a 21:00 call. Mediating that relationship is a category error. §10.6 provides the structural referral path, and it is expected to absorb a large share *[target: ~[40]% of Rung-2 escalations]* of what currently arrives as personality clash.

| **Trust cost** | Effort required to interpret a colleague charitably and to disagree safely | Time since last co-presence; cultural distance; hub asymmetry | Overlay T cadence, onboarding, pairing, facilitation, visible fairness in the time-zone ledger |

**Design rule.** Latency cost is bounded by geography; you can manage it but not eliminate it. **Context cost and trust cost are entirely self-inflicted** and are where the return on effort sits. A team that blames time zones for a context-cost problem will restructure its hiring and stay broken.

## §4 Latency architecture: response contracts and handoffs

### 4.1 The principle

In a co-located team, response latency is implicit and short, so no one specifies it. Distributed, the implicit contract is the single largest source of F1 — each party assumes the other's expectation. **Publish the contract.**

### 4.2 Response-latency classes *[targets — Gate 1 to calibrate per team]*

| Class | Meaning | Channel | Target response | Who may invoke |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L0 — Now** | Production down, safety, customer-critical | Paging / on-call | ≤[15] min | Anyone, per published severity criteria |
| **L1 — Same working day** | Blocked; work stops without an answer | Named channel, tagged "blocked" | ≤[4] working hours in the responder's day | Anyone, must state what is blocked |
| **L2 — Next working day** | Needed to plan, not to proceed | Team channel | ≤[1] working day | Default for team traffic |
| **L3 — This week** | Review, opinion, non-blocking input | Document comment / thread | ≤[3] working days | Default for cross-team traffic |
| **L4 — No response required** | Broadcast, FYI, archive | Announcement channel | None | Anyone |

**Three rules that make this real:**

1. **Latency is measured in the responder's working hours, never in wall-clock hours.** A question sent at 18:00 Stuttgart is not "overdue" at 09:00 Bengaluru. Publishing this eliminates a large fraction of perceived unresponsiveness — which is F1 presenting as F5.
2. **The sender declares the class; the sender owns the consequence of over-declaring.** Repeated false L1 is a Charter violation, not a personality trait. Gate 1 measures L1 invocation rate per head *[target: <[2]/week]*; a team above target has an ambiguity problem (F2) or an authority problem (F3), not an urgency problem.
3. **No class shorter than L1 exists outside on-call.** A team cannot norm its way into 15-minute expectations for ordinary work; that is how M1 deep focus dies and how the nearest-to-headquarters person becomes the default answerer.

### 4.3 The handoff packet

Where work crosses a time-zone boundary, the transfer is a **manufacturing handoff and should be engineered like one.** Free-text "here's where I got to" messages are the dominant source of rework in follow-the-sun teams.

**Required packet fields:**

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| **State** | What is done, in the receiver's terms, with links |
| **Next action** | The single next thing, phrased as a verb and an object |
| **Decisions taken** | With links to decision records (§6.2); prevents re-litigation |
| **Open questions, each with an owner and a latency class** | Prevents questions dying in the gap |
| **Blockers and who can clear them** | Names, not teams |
| **Do-not-touch** | What the receiver must not change without consulting; the single highest-value field, and the most often omitted |
| **Confidence** | Calibrated: "verified / believed / assumed." Distinguishes fact from inference across the handoff |

**Standard:** handoff packets are written **before** the sender's day ends, in the shared source of truth, not in chat. Gate 1 measures **handoff defect rate** — proportion of handoffs requiring clarification before the receiver can start *[target: <[10]%]*. This is the single best leading indicator of F1 and F2 and should be on the delivery dashboard.

A four-continent chain with three handoffs cannot be made fast by discipline alone. Named explicitly, because unnamed objectives get traded away silently.

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|

## §3 The Subsidiarity Rule and the three layers

> **Subsidiarity Rule:** Every decision about where and how work happens is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects — and no lower.

A decision affecting one team's week belongs to that team. A decision affecting statutory rights belongs to the country. A decision affecting whether two teams on different continents can ship together belongs to the centre. Pushing a decision *up* costs speed and fit; pushing it *down* costs coherence and manufactures local unfairness.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Spine** | Executive Committee | 8 commitments. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual review |
| **Country Dial** | Country lead + HR + Legal, with works council where applicable | Legal floor, stipend values, office footprint and format mix, planning band, local core hours, right-to-disconnect implementation, language of record | Semi-annual |
| **Team Charter** | Team lead with the team | Mode profile, together-time and its purpose, core overlap, response-time norms, meeting inventory, decision protocol, onboarding, inclusion check | Semi-annual, published |

## §4 Latency architecture: response contracts and handoffs

### 4.1 The principle

In a co-located team, response latency is implicit and short, so no one specifies it. Distributed, the implicit contract is the single largest source of F1 — each party assumes the other's expectation. **Publish the contract.**

### 4.2 Response-latency classes *[targets — Gate 1 to calibrate per team]*

| Class | Meaning | Channel | Target response | Who may invoke |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L0 — Now** | Production down, safety, customer-critical | Paging / on-call | ≤[15] min | Anyone, per published severity criteria |
| **L1 — Same working day** | Blocked; work stops without an answer | Named channel, tagged "blocked" | ≤[4] working hours in the responder's day | Anyone, must state what is blocked |
| **L2 — Next working day** | Needed to plan, not to proceed | Team channel | ≤[1] working day | Default for team traffic |
| **L3 — This week** | Review, opinion, non-blocking input | Document comment / thread | ≤[3] working days | Default for cross-team traffic |
| **L4 — No response required** | Broadcast, FYI, archive | Announcement channel | None | Anyone |

**Three rules that make this real:**

1. **Latency is measured in the responder's working hours, never in wall-clock hours.** A question sent at 18:00 Stuttgart is not "overdue" at 09:00 Bengaluru. Publishing this eliminates a large fraction of perceived unresponsiveness — which is F1 presenting as F5.
2. **The sender declares the class; the sender owns the consequence of over-declaring.** Repeated false L1 is a Charter violation, not a personality trait. Gate 1 measures L1 invocation rate per head *[target: <[2]/week]*; a team above target has an ambiguity problem (F2) or an authority problem (F3), not an urgency problem.
3. **No class shorter than L1 exists outside on-call.** A team cannot norm its way into 15-minute expectations for ordinary work; that is how M1 deep focus dies and how the nearest-to-headquarters person becomes the default answerer.

### 4.3 The handoff packet

Where work crosses a time-zone boundary, the transfer is a **manufacturing handoff and should be engineered like one.** Free-text "here's where I got to" messages are the dominant source of rework in follow-the-sun teams.

**Required packet fields:**

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| **State** | What is done, in the receiver's terms, with links |
| **Next action** | The single next thing, phrased as a verb and an object |
| **Decisions taken** | With links to decision records (§6.2); prevents re-litigation |
| **Open questions, each with an owner and a latency class** | Prevents questions dying in the gap |
| **Blockers and who can clear them** | Names, not teams |
| **Do-not-touch** | What the receiver must not change without consulting; the single highest-value field, and the most often omitted |
| **Confidence** | Calibrated: "verified / believed / assumed." Distinguishes fact from inference across the handoff |

**Standard:** handoff packets are written **before** the sender's day ends, in the shared source of truth, not in chat. Gate 1 measures **handoff defect rate** — proportion of handoffs requiring clarification before the receiver can start *[target: <[10]%]*. This is the single best leading indicator of F1 and F2 and should be on the delivery dashboard.

### 4.4 Reduce hops before you reduce latency

A four-continent chain with three handoffs cannot be made fast by discipline alone. Before optimising handoffs, ask whether the work can be **re-sliced so that a decision-complete unit sits inside one time zone.** Vertical ownership of a whole capability by one region beats horizontal layer-ownership across three, almost always. This is an architecture and staffing decision, and it belongs to the programme owner, not the team lead — see §16.

## The answer in one paragraph

**These teams do not have a communication problem. They have an architecture problem that presents as a communication problem, and the standard response — more channels, more standups, more tooling — reliably makes it worse.** "Delays and misunderstandings" is symptom vocabulary; underneath it sit **seven distinct failure modes** — latency, ambiguity, decision re-litigation, unshared time-zone tax, cultural misread, relational deficit, and language asymmetry (§1) — each with a different and sometimes opposite remedy. So the first deliverable is not a practice; it is a **triage instrument** that tells a team which failure mode it actually has, with a confirming measurement for each (§3). The remedies are then: **(a)** a published **response-latency contract** measured in the *responder's* working hours, plus engineered **handoff packets** borrowed wholesale from shift-handover practice in our own plants (§5); **(b)** **deliberate time-zone architecture** — one of four topologies chosen on the arithmetic, not inherited from hiring history, and the arithmetic is unforgiving: our own named hubs of Bengaluru, Stuttgart and Salt Lake City share **no hour of common working time at all** (§6.2), which means "add a daily all-hands standup" is not a hard option but an impossible one; **(c)** a **federated source of truth** — canonical index plus jurisdictionally sited stores — because a single global repository is illegal or unreachable in several of our markets and S8 is a hard gate (§7.1); **(d)** **language architecture treated as an equity mechanism**, not an etiquette note (§8.1); **(e)** a **Team Culture Map** built from individual self-description and never from a country-to-dimension lookup table (§8.2); **(f)** **trust as funded capacity** with a named rule against unsupported solo-in-region placement (§10); and **(g)** a **five-rung conflict ladder with timeboxes and a structural screen at every rung**, on the working hypothesis that a large share of what arrives as personality clash is a decision-rights defect wearing a face (§11). Two disciplines run through all of it: every measurement is a **team-level diagnostic and is prohibited as an individual performance input** (§5.5), and every load-bearing empirical claim is **labelled as a hypothesis with a Gate 1 test** (§1.3), because the parent framework holds itself to that standard and a companion document that does not will not be believed.

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

"Communication delays and occasional misunderstandings" is a **composite symptom**. Treated as one thing it attracts one intervention — usually a tool, sometimes a mandate to overlap — and both fail, because at least seven mechanisms are in play and several of them have opposite remedies. Adding synchronous contact helps a team with a relational deficit and actively harms a team with an ambiguity problem, because it moves specification back into unrecorded speech.

### 1.1 The seven failure modes

| # | Failure mode | What it looks like | What it actually is | Wrong fix | Right fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **F1** | **Latency** | "Asked Tuesday, answered Friday, shipped a week late" | No published response contract; questions batched into the wrong channel | Force overlap; add standups | Response-latency classes + handoff packets (§5) |
| **F2** | **Ambiguity** | Two sites built to two readings of the same sentence | Specification and commitment language are uncalibrated | "Communicate more" | Commitment Language Standard + Severity Lexicon + spec templates (§7.4) |
| **F3** | **Decision re-litigation** | The same decision made three times in three regions | Decisions unwritten, or written where the other region cannot find them | More meetings | Decision records + federated source of truth + DRI naming (§7.2–7.3) |
| **F4** | **Unshared time-zone tax** | One region always on the 22:00 call; that region goes quiet, then attrites | A distributional injustice, not an attitude problem | Resilience training | Topology choice + rotation + unsociable-hours ledger (§6) |
| **F5** | **Cultural misread** | Silence read as consent; directness read as contempt; escalation read as betrayal | Divergent, unwritten norms about feedback, hierarchy, disagreement and silence | Awareness e-learning | Team Culture Map → written team norms (§8.2) |
| **F6** | **Relational deficit** | Text read in the least charitable available tone | Insufficient relational credit to absorb ordinary friction | Virtual happy hours | Funded Overlay T cadence + onboarding redesign (§10) |
| **F7** | **Language asymmetry** | The same three fluent speakers decide everything; others "had no comments" | Fast idiomatic synchronous speech is a competence tax on non-native speakers, and it silently reallocates influence | Ask people to speak up | Language architecture: written-first as equaliser, no-idiom norms, captions and transcripts by default, speaking-order rotation, interpretation budget (§8.1) |

F7 was absent from v1.0 and is the most consequential addition. It is separate from F5 because the remedies are different and cheaper: F5 requires negotiated norms, F7 requires channel and facilitation design. Conflating them produces culture training where a caption track and a written agenda would have done more.

### 1.2 Three corollaries

**Corollary 1 — Volume is not the variable.** Our working expectation **[H1]** is that teams reporting the worst communication show *higher*, not lower, message and meeting volume. Adding channels to a team suffering F2 or F3 is actively harmful: ambiguity replicates and re-litigation accelerates. This is a testable claim, not a slogan, and §3 gives the measurement.

*(The v1.0 formulation "more communication is the disease's most common presentation" is withdrawn as logically confused. The precise claim is narrower and survives scrutiny: **excess undifferentiated volume is a symptom that is routinely mistaken for the cure.** This document itself prescribes a substantial quantity of new communication norms; the defence is that norms reduce volume by removing the need to negotiate expectations transaction by transaction.)*

**Corollary 2 — Distance does not create misunderstanding; it removes the cheap repair.** Co-located teams misunderstand each other constantly and repair it in four seconds at a desk. Distributed teams discover the same misunderstanding a week later, downstream, expensive. Our expectation **[H2]** is that the underlying misunderstanding *rate* is similar and the *detection latency* is what differs by an order of magnitude.

> **Therefore the design goal is not fewer misunderstandings. It is shorter time-to-detection.**

Read every practice in §5 and §7 as detection-latency reduction, not defect-rate reduction. This single reframe changes what you build: you stop trying to write perfect specifications and start building cheap, fast contradiction detectors — confidence labels, do-not-touch fields, decision records that a distant reader trips over, handoff packets that fail loudly.

**Corollary 3 — Most reported interpersonal conflict in cross-border teams is structural.** An engineer who believes a counterpart is obstructive is usually looking at a person with contradictory instructions from a second reporting line, no decision right over the thing being asked of them, and a 21:00 call. Mediating that relationship is a category error: it asks two people to be nicer about a defect neither of them owns.

*Correcting v1.0:* no target is set on this share. Setting a target on a *diagnostic classification* creates pressure to reclassify in order to hit it, which is precisely the failure we are trying to prevent. Instead: the structural-screen outcome (§11.4) is **measured and reported**, with a **monitored range** *[expected range 25–55% of Rung-2 escalations — Gate 1 to establish the baseline]*.
